concepts.title: Magnitude and Direction of a 2D Vector
concepts.definition: A two-dimensional vector can be completely written as its mutually orthogonal rectangular components, whose root sum of squares gives its overall size and whose ratio gives its angular orientation.
concepts.formula: magnitude = sqrt(x_comp**2 + y_comp**2), tan_theta = y_comp / x_comp
concepts.key_idea: The Euclidean length of perpendicular components determines the total vector magnitude.
question_patterns: find the magnitude of the vector given its components
calculate the resultant speed from horizontal and vertical components
what is the magnitude of velocity given vx and vy
determine the overall vector size from perpendicular components
work out the value using magnitude and direction of a 2d vector

solution_steps.explain: Square each perpendicular component and add them together
Magnitude is the square root of the sum of squares
The direction is the arctangent of the ratio of vertical to horizontal component

concepts.title: Resultant of Two Perpendicular Vectors
concepts.definition: When two physical vectors act at right angles to one another, their combined effect has a magnitude given by the Pythagorean sum of individual magnitudes.
concepts.key_idea: For orthogonal vectors, the cosine cross-term vanishes leaving the square root of the sum of squares.

solution_steps.explain: Compute sum of squares of vector A and vector B
The resultant magnitude is the square root of the sum of squares
The angle of the resultant with the horizontal is the arctangent of the ratio of the two perpendicular magnitudes

concepts.title: Two-Dimensional Kinematics with Constant Acceleration
concepts.definition: Motion in two dimensions under uniform acceleration separates into two independent straight-line motions along orthogonal axes.
concepts.formula: x = x0 + vox*t + 0.5*ax*t**2, y = y0 + voy*t + 0.5*ay*t**2
concepts.key_idea: Orthogonal coordinates evolve independently according to one-dimensional kinematic laws.

concepts.title: Time of Flight of a Projectile
concepts.definition: The total duration an airborne object spends traversing its parabolic trajectory before returning to its launch elevation.
concepts.key_idea: Time in air depends solely on the vertical launch velocity component and gravitational acceleration.
question_patterns: find the time of flight of a projectile
calculate the total time taken by a thrown ball to return to ground level

solution_steps.explain: Multiply launch speed by sine of launch angle
Double the vertical speed and divide by acceleration due to gravity

solution_steps.action: compute time to reach maximum height
solution_steps.explain: The time to reach the peak is half the total time of flight since the upward and downward phases are symmetric

worked_examples.question: Solve a typical question involving time of flight of a projectile.

concepts.title: Maximum Height of a Projectile
concepts.definition: The highest vertical altitude reached by a projectile during flight, occurring when the vertical velocity component momentarily reaches zero.
concepts.key_idea: The peak altitude is governed exclusively by the initial vertical velocity component.
question_patterns: calculate the maximum height reached by a projectile

solution_steps.explain: Multiply initial velocity by sine of elevation angle
Square vertical velocity component and divide by twice gravitational acceleration

solution_steps.action: compute time to reach maximum height
solution_steps.explain: The time to reach the peak equals the vertical velocity component divided by gravitational acceleration

worked_examples.solution: Step 1: calculate vertical velocity component. Step 2: compute maximum height. Step 3: compute time to reach maximum height. Working: v0 * sin_theta, (voy**2) / (2 * g), voy / g.

concepts.title: Horizontal Range of a Projectile
concepts.definition: The total horizontal span traversed by a projectile from its launch position to the point where it returns to the projection level.
concepts.formula: R = (v0**2 * sin_2theta) / g, R_max = v0**2 / g
concepts.key_idea: Range is maximized at an launch angle of 45 degrees where sin(2*theta) equals unity.
question_patterns: find the horizontal range of a projectile
calculate the distance from thrower where the ball lands

solution_steps.explain: Square the projection speed

solution_steps.action: multiply by trigonometric factor and divide by g
solution_steps.explain: Multiply squared speed by sin(2*theta) and divide by g
The maximum range occurs at 45 degrees where sin(2*theta) equals one, giving v0 squared divided by g

concepts.title: Centripetal Acceleration from Speed and Radius
concepts.definition: The inward radial acceleration felt by a body traveling along a circular trajectory at constant speed.
concepts.key_idea: Continuously redirecting the velocity vector toward the circle's centre produces radial acceleration.
question_patterns: find the centripetal acceleration of an object in circular motion

solution_steps.explain: Compute the square of tangential velocity
Divide squared speed by radius of circular path
Multiply centripetal acceleration by the mass of the object to obtain the inward force

worked_examples.question: Solve a typical question involving centripetal acceleration from speed and radius.
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: square the linear speed. Step 2: divide by orbital radius. Step 3: compute centripetal force. Working: speed**2, v_sq / radius, mass * centripetal_acc.
worked_examples.answer: Centripetal Acceleration from Speed and Radius applied step by step gives the required result.

concepts.title: Centripetal Acceleration in terms of Frequency and Radius
concepts.definition: Centripetal acceleration expressed in terms of the rate of revolution or rotational frequency and circular radius.
concepts.key_idea: Circular acceleration scales with the square of rotation rate and directly with path radius.
